666.title: Janus looks both ways
666.hook: the Romans named January for Janus, who looks backward and forward
666.howItsDone: Some people mark a new year or a transition by deliberately looking back at what they learned and forward to one clear step, then returning attention to the present.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a new year, and Seneca's first letter. Your line was begin now. Did the small first step happen, or is it still waiting on the calendar? Day six hundred sixty-six.

Stand in a doorway for a moment. Behind you, the room you're leaving. In front, the room you're walking into. For a second you're in neither, and you can see both. Ancient Romans gave that spot its own god. His name was Janus, and on coins and statues he has two faces, one looking back and one looking forward. The doorway, the gate and the first day of the year all belonged to him. Our word January still carries his name.
screen: `STANDING IN A DOORWAY.` → `TWO FACES, BACK AND FORWARD.` → `JANUARY: JANUS'S MONTH.`

segments.voice: First, who he was to the Romans. Janus was the god of beginnings and passages: doors, gates, the start of things. In Roman worship his name was often called first in prayers, before other gods, because he stood at the opening. The poet Ovid, in his poem on the Roman calendar, has Janus explain his two faces like a doorkeeper who watches both the street and the house. Second, a famous door. In Rome, the gates of a small shrine to Janus were open in wartime and closed in peace. They were rarely closed. The emperor Augustus boasted that they'd been shut three times in his rule. Third, what a Stoic would make of the two faces. Seneca and Marcus both warned about living in the past or the future. Seneca observes that fear and hope march together, and both come from a mind that leans ahead instead of standing in the present. Marcus reminds himself that the only life anyone loses is the moment they're living now. So a Stoic might look at Janus and say: look both ways, yes, but don't move into either room. Fourth, how to look well. Look back to learn, not to replay. What went right? What would you do differently? Look forward to prepare, not to worry. What is one thing to do next? Then step through the doorway into the room that's real, which is this one. Janus himself stands in the threshold, after all, not in the past or the future.
screen: `JANUS: GOD OF DOORS AND BEGINNINGS.` · `GATES SHUT ONLY IN PEACETIME.` · `DON'T MOVE INTO EITHER ROOM.` · `BACK TO LEARN, AHEAD TO PREPARE.` · then, large: `BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand in a real doorway. If not, picture one. Look back first: think of the last few months. Find one thing you learned, just one, and let it be enough. Now turn and look forward: the next few months. Find one thing you want to do, small and clear. Then come back to the doorway itself. Feel your feet. This is the threshold, the only place you ever actually stand. The bell holds the time.
Janus, the Roman god of doorways and beginnings, with one face to the past and one to the future, who gave January its name. Today's word.
Your line: both ways. Next time you pass through a door today, glance back once to learn, forward once to prepare, and then walk on. Day six hundred sixty-six.

667.title: The spring equinox
667.hook: day and night equal: an image of balance
667.howItsDone: Many cultures mark the spring equinox with new-year or spring festivals; some people use it as a moment to look at the balance of work, rest and company in their lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janus in the doorway, one face back and one forward. Your line was both ways. Did a doorway remind you to look back once, then forward once? Day six hundred sixty-seven.

Twice a year, the sun, as seen from Earth, crosses the line of the equator, and for a day the whole planet, from Oslo to Cape Town, gets roughly the same amount of light and dark. Twelve hours, give or take. In March, for the northern half of the world, the light is winning from here on. Many peoples have marked it: Nowruz, the Persian new year, begins at that moment, and the date of Easter is still reckoned from a spring equinox fixed at March 21. Today, on the porch, we look at the spring equinox as a picture, and ask what it shows.
screen: `THE SUN CROSSES THE EQUATOR.` → `TWELVE HOURS, GIVE OR TAKE.` → `A PICTURE OF BALANCE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Equinox comes from Latin, aequinoctium: equal night. And a small surprise: it isn't exactly equal. Because the sun is a disk, not a point, and the air bends its light, most places get a few minutes more day than night on the equinox itself. The truly equal day comes a little before it in spring. Balance in nature is close, not perfect. Second, the Stoic picture of balance. Seneca, writing to his friend Serenus about peace of mind, gives a list of alternations. Mix solitude and company: being alone makes us long for people, and people make us long to be alone, and each cures the other. Give the mind rest, he says, the way you'd let a field lie fallow, because ground forced to produce every year wears out. He mentions that Socrates wasn't ashamed to play with small children. Third, what that balance isn't. It isn't a perfect fifty-fifty schedule, like the equinox that's never quite exact. It's noticing which way you've tipped. Too much work, not enough rest. Too many people, not enough quiet. Too much screen, not enough sky. Fourth, why spring is a good time to check. Things are about to grow fast. Days lengthen. Plans multiply. Before the light runs away with you, the equinox stands still for a day and says: here is what even looks like. Now choose where to add a little light, and where to let a little dark stay.
screen: `AEQUINOCTIUM: EQUAL NIGHT, NEARLY.` · `SOLITUDE AND COMPANY, WORK AND REST.` · `NOTICE WHICH WAY YOU'VE TIPPED.` · `CHECK BEFORE THE LIGHT RUNS AWAY.` · then, large: `EQUAL LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Picture your ordinary day as a scale. On one side, everything that fills it: work, errands, screens, people. On the other: rest, quiet, play, time outside. Which side hangs lower? Don't scold yourself; just see it. Now choose one small thing to move across. Ten minutes of quiet. One walk without your phone. One call to a friend if you've been alone too much. Picture the scale shifting, just slightly. The bell holds the time.
Aequinoctium, Latin for equal night, the root of the word equinox, when day and night come close to even. Today's word.
Your line: equal light. Move the one small thing you chose across the scale today, and notice how the day feels with it there. Day six hundred sixty-seven.

668.title: A neighbor's day of atonement
668.hook: Jews keep Yom Kippur as a day of fasting and repentance, in their own way and with their own meaning
668.howItsDone: On Yom Kippur many Jews fast from one evening until nightfall the next and spend much of the day in synagogue prayer; in the days before it, many seek out people they have wronged to apologize.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the spring equinox, aequinoctium, and a scale that's never perfectly even. Your line was equal light. Did one small thing move across to the lighter side? Day six hundred sixty-eight.

One autumn evening, synagogues fill for a day the Torah sets apart. Some people wear white. Those who keep the fast eat nothing and drink nothing from that evening until the stars come out the next night, when a long blast of the ram's horn ends the day. This is Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. Leviticus calls it a sabbath of solemn rest. It isn't ours to borrow. But a good neighbor can learn what it is, and let it ask a question of their own life.
screen: `AN AUTUMN EVENING, SYNAGOGUES FILL.` → `EVENING TO NIGHTFALL, NO FOOD OR WATER.` → `A NEIGHBOR'S HOLY DAY.`

segments.voice: First, the source. In the book of Leviticus, the tenth day of the seventh month is set apart. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, the people are told: "ye shall afflict your souls." Jewish tradition has long understood that as fasting and holding back from certain comforts, and the day is spent largely in prayer, from the evening service called Kol Nidre to the closing service, Neilah. Second, the inner work. The Hebrew word at its center is teshuvah, often translated repentance, though it comes from the root for returning. Turning back. Jewish teachers, Maimonides among them, describe recognizing a wrong, regretting it, setting it right where possible, and resolving to do differently. Third, a teaching about other people. The Mishnah, an early collection of Jewish law, says Yom Kippur brings atonement for wrongs between a person and God, but for wrongs between one person and another, not until you've made peace with the person you wronged. So it's a custom, in the days before it, to call, write and apologize. The day doesn't skip the phone call. Fourth, what a neighbor can take, carefully. Not the fast, not the prayers, not the meaning, which belong to the people who keep it. Only the question it leaves in the air for anyone watching with respect: have I looked honestly at my year? Is there someone I owe a word to? The Stoics had their own version, Seneca's nightly review, which we'll meet again soon. That nightly look is a different thing, from a different place, and it doesn't stand in for this one.
screen: `LEVITICUS: YE SHALL AFFLICT YOUR SOULS.` · `TESHUVAH: TURNING BACK.` · `WRONGED A PERSON? MAKE PEACE FIRST.` · `A NEIGHBOR'S QUESTION, NOT A BORROWING.` · then, large: `HONEST REVIEW.`

segments.voice: In your own way, look back over the past year. Not to punish yourself. Just to see. Where did you do well? Let that count. Where did you fall short of who you meant to be? Name one place, plainly. Is there a person connected to it? If there is, picture them, and ask whether a word from you, an apology or a thank-you, might be owed. You don't have to decide now. Just let the honest picture stand. The bell holds the time.
Teshuvah, the Hebrew word at the heart of Yom Kippur, meaning turning back: recognizing a wrong, regretting it, and resolving to do differently. Today's word.
Your line: honest review. If one person came to mind in the practice, consider sending them a short, honest message today. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

669.title: The summer solstice
669.hook: the longest day, and Marcus would note it passes too
669.howItsDone: Many cultures mark midsummer with bonfires, outdoor gatherings or staying up through the short night; some readers of Marcus use the longest day as a reminder to enjoy what is passing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a neighbor's day of atonement, teshuvah, and a question it leaves for anyone watching with respect. Your line was honest review. Did one honest look, or one honest message, happen? Day six hundred sixty-nine.

Nine-thirty at night, and it's still light enough to read on the back step. Kids are still out on bikes. Somebody's grill is still going. In the far north, in places like northern Norway, the sun doesn't set at all this time of year. The summer solstice: the longest day in the northern half of the world. People have lit bonfires for it, danced around poles for it, stayed up all night for it. The light seems like it could go on forever. Marcus Aurelius would enjoy it, and then gently remind himself of one thing.
screen: `STILL LIGHT AT NINE-THIRTY.` → `THE LONGEST DAY.` → `IT SEEMS TO GO ON FOREVER.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Solstice comes from Latin, solstitium: the sun standing still. For days around it, the sun seems to rise and set at almost the same points on the horizon, as if pausing at the top of its climb before turning back. Second, the pause is the turn. From tomorrow, in the north, the days begin to shorten, a little at a time. The peak of the light and the start of its going are the same moment. Third, Marcus. He writes in the Meditations that time is like a river made of things that happen, a strong current: as soon as something is seen, it's swept away, and something else takes its place, and that too will be carried off. He also tells himself to think often about how fast everything that exists and comes into being is carried past and out of sight. To some readers that sounds bleak. But read beside his other notes, it's not a reason to hold back from enjoying things. It's a reason to enjoy them now, while they're here, without trying to clamp them in place. Fourth, the solstice as practice. A long day can seem so roomy that it slips by unnoticed. Marcus's reminder turns that around: because it's passing, it's worth being out in. Long light, still passing. Both halves are true, and the second makes the first worth more.
screen: `SOLSTITIUM: THE SUN STANDING STILL.` · `THE PEAK IS ALSO THE TURN.` · `A RIVER OF THINGS, SWEPT PAST.` · `PASSING, SO WORTH BEING OUT IN.` · then, large: `LONG LIGHT, STILL PASSING.`

segments.voice: If you can, go outside, or sit by a window with the most sky you can find. Look at the light as it is right now. Its color. Where the shadows fall. How warm or cool the air is. Let yourself enjoy it fully, without planning anything. Then, quietly, notice that this exact light is already changing, moving across the wall, the ground, your hand. Enjoy it anyway, and partly because it's passing. The bell holds the time.
Solstitium, Latin for the sun standing still, the root of solstice, the longest day when the light pauses before it turns. Today's word.
Your line: long light, still passing. Spend ten minutes of today's light outdoors on purpose, not on the way to anywhere. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

670.title: The ripe olive
670.hook: Marcus pictures an olive falling ripe, blessing the tree that bore it (Meditations 4.48)
670.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus use the image of the ripe olive to reflect on accepting life's seasons, and to eat food in season with attention and thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the summer solstice, solstitium, the longest day, already turning. Your line was long light, still passing. Did you spend ten minutes outdoors on purpose? Day six hundred seventy.

If you've ever stood under an olive tree in the fall, in Greece or Italy or California, you might have seen it: fruit dropping on its own, a soft tap on the ground, then another. Nobody shook the branch. The olive was simply ready. For people around the ancient Mediterranean, the olive was everywhere: food, lamp oil, medicine, the oil rubbed on athletes. And in book four of his notebook, at the end of a long, sober passage, he reaches for one to say something hard in a gentle way.
screen: `A SOFT TAP ON THE GROUND.` → `FOOD, LAMPLIGHT, MEDICINE.` → `MARCUS REACHES FOR AN OLIVE.`

segments.voice: First, the long passage. Marcus lists people who are gone: doctors who frowned over many patients and then died themselves, astrologers who predicted others' deaths, philosophers who argued about immortality, great generals, whole cities. He isn't being morbid. He's reminding himself, again, how short and shared a human life is. Second, the olive. Then he turns. Pass through this little space of time in keeping with nature, he writes, and end the journey content, the way a ripe olive falls, blessing nature that produced it, and thanking the tree it grew on. A falling olive doesn't cling. It doesn't curse the branch. It drops in its season, grateful. Third, what ripe means. For Marcus, everything in nature has its time: being young, growing up, getting gray, and also dying. Elsewhere he says to treat death as one of the works of nature, like teething or a beard coming in. Some people find comfort in that; others find it hard. Both are honest reactions, and the Meditations don't demand that you feel one way about it. Fourth, the smaller lesson. The olive is in season. Not early, not forced, not late, and it gives thanks for what grew it. Marcus means it as a way to end. It can also be a way to eat: a fruit picked in its own month carries the weather and the soil of the place it came from. So today the porch asks something light of you: taste one thing that's ripe right now, and let a little thanks go back to where it grew.
screen: `DOCTORS, GENERALS, WHOLE CITIES, GONE.` · `FALL LIKE A RIPE OLIVE, GRATEFUL.` · `EVERYTHING IN NATURE HAS ITS TIME.` · `TASTE WHAT'S RIPE, THANK THE TREE.` · then, large: `IN SEASON.`

segments.voice: If you have something in season near you, a piece of fruit, a vegetable, even a handful of nuts, hold it. If not, picture one. Look at it closely. Think of the plant it came from, the weather that ripened it, the hands that picked and carried it. If it's in front of you, taste it slowly. Let one silent thank-you go back to the tree, or the field, or the people. Then just sit with the taste. The bell holds the time.
Ripe olive, Marcus's picture of a life that ends in its season, falling without clinging, grateful to the tree that bore it. Today's word.
Your line: in season. Eat one thing today that's ripe where you live right now, and notice what it tastes like when it's on time. Day six hundred seventy.

671.title: The autumn equinox
671.hook: balance again, and the light begins to shorten
671.howItsDone: Many cultures hold harvest festivals around the autumn equinox; some readers of the Stoics mark it with a dusk walk and a reflection on the seasons of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ripe olive, falling in its season and thanking the tree. Your line was in season. What did you taste that was ripe right now? Day six hundred seventy-one.

It shows up first at dinner. In August, dinner was eaten in daylight. Now the kitchen light is on before the pasta's done. The mornings are cooler. The trees on your street have a few yellow leaves, like the first gray hairs. Back in the spring, on the porch, we stood at the equinox and watched the light begin to win. Today the scale balances again, day and night nearly even. But this time, from here, in the north, the dark grows. The autumn equinox: the same balance, facing the other way.
screen: `THE KITCHEN LIGHT, ON EARLIER.` → `A FEW YELLOW LEAVES.` → `THE SAME BALANCE, FACING THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. Astronomically, it's the mirror of spring: the sun crosses the equator heading south, and the northern days grow shorter than the nights. Same balance, different direction. Some people feel it in their mood, a slight heaviness as evenings close in. That's real, and it's worth being gentle with. Second, Seneca in autumn. In his twelfth letter, he visits his country house and grumbles to the caretaker that the old plane trees look neglected. The caretaker says he's doing all he can; the trees are just old. Then Seneca remembers: he planted them himself. The trees are simply his age. And then the letter turns: he says we should welcome and love old age, because it is full of pleasure if you know how to use it. Fruit, he says, is most welcome when it's almost over. Third, the Stoic view of turnings. For Seneca and Marcus, nature's cycles aren't something going wrong. Seasons turn, people age, the light comes and goes, and all of it belongs to the same whole. That doesn't mean you have to like the shorter days. It means you can stop treating them as a mistake. Fourth, what autumn offers. The best light of the year, some say: low, gold, long shadows. Harvest. A slower pace. The turning isn't only loss. It's a different kind of day, with its own gifts, the way the later part of a life has its own. Dusk shows it plainly, when day and night meet in the same sky.
screen: `THE MIRROR OF SPRING.` · `SENECA'S OLD PLANE TREES.` · `TURNINGS AREN'T MISTAKES.` · `A DIFFERENT DAY, WITH ITS OWN GIFTS.` · then, large: `THE TURNING.`

segments.voice: If it's near evening, step outside, or to a window, and watch the light go. If it's earlier, picture a dusk you remember. Notice the colors as the day drains out of the sky. The sounds changing. The air cooling. Don't hurry it, and don't hold on to it. Let the day turn into evening while you watch. If a feeling of loss comes, let it be there. If a feeling of rest comes, let that be there too. The bell holds the time.
Autumn equinox, when day and night return to balance but the light begins to shorten, a turning with its own gifts. Today's word.
Your line: the turning. Take a short walk at dusk this evening, and notice one thing the turning season gives rather than takes. Day six hundred seventy-one.

672.title: Saturnalia, roles reversed
672.hook: the Roman midwinter festival turned roles upside down; Seneca stayed sober and practiced poverty (Letters 18)
672.howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca mark busy festive seasons by keeping a few plain days, and by giving thanks or gifts to the people who serve them through the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the autumn equinox, and Seneca laughing at his own old trees. Your line was the turning. Did you catch the dusk, and one thing the season gave? Day six hundred seventy-two, the end of a week.

Rome, mid-December. The streets are loud. People have swapped their formal togas for loose, bright dinner clothes. Shops are selling little clay figures and wax candles to give as presents. Gambling, usually frowned on, is allowed in public. In some households, ancient writers tell us, the strangest thing of all: for the feast, the enslaved people of the house are served, or sit at table with the family, and the masters wait on them. It's the Saturnalia, the festival of the god Saturn. And Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius, has some thoughts about how to spend it.
screen: `ROME, MID-DECEMBER.` → `CANDLES, CLAY FIGURES, DICE.` → `THE MASTERS SERVE.`

segments.voice: First, the festival. The Saturnalia began on December seventeenth and grew over time to several days. Romans remembered Saturn's reign as a golden age, before rich and poor, when everyone was equal. For a few days, the festival played at that: freedom of speech, gifts, and roles turned upside down. It was a game, and the next week everything went back. Rome was a slave society, and we should say that plainly. But the game itself admitted something: the order of things wasn't the only possible one. Second, Seneca's letter. It's December, he writes, and the whole city is sweating with celebration. Should we join in, or stay apart? His answer is balanced: don't make a show of refusing, but don't lose yourself. Keep a sober head while others are drunk. Third, his surprising suggestion. While everyone feasts, he says, set aside a few days to live on the plainest, cheapest food and in rough clothing, and ask yourself: is this what I was afraid of? Rich people, he says, sometimes did this for fun; he means it as training, so that poverty, if it ever came, would hold no terror. Fourth, the reversal that lasts. Seneca wrote another letter arguing that the people who serve us are human beings like us, born of the same seed, under the same sky. Saturnalia flipped roles for a day. A Stoic tries to keep a little of that all year: seeing the person who brings your coffee, cleans the office, delivers the box, as fully a person, and acting like it. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: both ways. Equal light. Honest review. Long light, still passing. In season. The turning. Roles reversed.
screen: `SATURN'S GOLDEN AGE, PLAYED FOR DAYS.` · `SOBER WHILE THE CITY CELEBRATES.` · `PLAIN FOOD: IS THIS WHAT I FEARED?` · `THE PEOPLE WHO SERVE US ARE PEOPLE.` · then, large: `ROLES REVERSED.`

segments.voice: Think of the people who serve you in an ordinary week. The person at the counter. The driver. The cleaner. The teacher. Someone at home who does more than their share. Picture one of them clearly, their face, their voice. Imagine, just for a moment, that the roles were reversed and you were doing their work for them. How would you want to be treated? Then choose one small thing you could give them: a real thank-you, a tip, a kindness. The bell holds the time.
Saturnalia: the Roman midwinter festival when roles were reversed, and for Seneca a time to stay sober, practice simplicity, and remember who serves us. Today's word.
Your line: roles reversed. Give something today, even small, to someone who usually serves you, and look them in the eye when you do. Day six hundred seventy-two.

myth: Seneca told Lucilius to make a show of refusing the festival
he advised not standing out, but keeping a sober head.
at the Saturnalia, masters sometimes served the enslaved at the feast
roles were turned upside down for the festival.
Seneca suggested a few days of plain food and rough clothes as training
so that poverty would hold no terror.

fork.setup: you're Lucilius, and the whole city is feasting for the Saturnalia. what does Seneca advise?
options: lock yourself away in protest
join in, but keep a sober head
drink more than anyone
fork.reveal: Letter 18: don't make yourself conspicuous by refusing, but don't lose yourself either; and try a few plain days.

trapdoor: what you thought: Saturnalia was just an ancient Roman party.
what it means: it reversed roles for a few days, recalling a golden age of equality; Seneca used it for sobriety and simplicity.

what a scholar hears: Letters 18 opens in December with the city in a sweat; Letters 47 argues that slaves are human beings born of the same seed; Macrobius describes masters serving slaves at the feast.
